## Problem 7.1: Adiabatic mixing revisited — including the enthalpy of solution

Problem 5.1 treated a well-insulated, steady-state mixing vessel and **neglected the
enthalpy of mixing**. Revisit it now with that assumption removed. The streams are
unchanged:

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
| Stream | Fluid | $\dot{m}$ (kg s$^{-1}$) | $T$ ($^\circ$C) | $C_P$ (kJ kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$) | $M$ (g mol$^{-1}$) |
|---|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| A | Ethanol | 1.50 | 20 | 2.44 | 46.07 |
| B | Water   | 0.80 | 75 | 4.18 | 18.02 |
:::

There is no heat loss and no shaft work. The enthalpy of mixing for ethanol–water at
25 $^\circ$C, per mole of *mixture*, is:

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
| $x_{ethanol}$ | 0.10 | 0.20 | 0.30 | 0.40 | 0.50 | 0.60 | 0.80 |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $\Delta H_{mix}$ (J mol$^{-1}$) | $-460$ | $-680$ | $-775$ | $-770$ | $-710$ | $-615$ | $-370$ |
:::

::: {.incremental}
(a) Find the composition of the outlet stream, as a mole fraction of ethanol.
(b) Determine the rate at which enthalpy is released by mixing, in kW.
(c) Using a reference state of the **pure liquids at 20 $^\circ$C**, find the outlet
    temperature.
(d) Compare with the answer obtained in Problem 5.1 and comment on whether neglecting
    the enthalpy of mixing was a reasonable assumption.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Solution"}

**System and assumptions**

The system is the mixing vessel. Steady state ($d(m_{sys}H_{sys})/dt = 0$), adiabatic
($\dot{Q}=0$), no shaft work ($\dot{W}=0$). The general balance

$$\frac{d(m_{sys}H_{sys})}{dt} = \sum \dot{m}_{in}H_{in} - \sum \dot{m}_{out}H_{out} + \dot{Q} + \dot{W}$$

reduces to

$$\sum \dot{m}_{in}H_{in} = \sum \dot{m}_{out}H_{out}$$

**Choice of reference state.** The composition changes across the system — pure liquids
enter, a mixture leaves — so a *solution* reference state cannot be used. Take the
**pure liquids at 20 $^\circ$C**. Every inlet species is then at its reference state, and
the mixing enthalpy must appear explicitly in the outlet term.

**(a) Outlet composition**

$$\dot{n}_{ethanol} = \frac{1500}{46.07} = 32.56\ \text{mol s}^{-1}
\qquad
\dot{n}_{water} = \frac{800}{18.02} = 44.40\ \text{mol s}^{-1}$$

$$\dot{n}_{total} = 76.96\ \text{mol s}^{-1}$$

$$x_{ethanol} = \frac{32.56}{76.96} = 0.423$$

The outlet is a single liquid stream of 2.30 kg s$^{-1}$ at $x_{ethanol} = 0.423$
(a mass fraction of $1.50/2.30 = 0.652$ — the two are not interchangeable, and the table
is given on a mole basis).

**(b) Rate of enthalpy release on mixing**

Interpolate the table linearly between $x = 0.40$ and $x = 0.50$:

$$\Delta H_{mix} = -770 + \frac{0.423 - 0.40}{0.50 - 0.40}\left(-710 - (-770)\right)
= -770 + 0.23(60) = -756\ \text{J mol}^{-1}$$

$\Delta H_{mix}$ is **intensive** — per mole of mixture. Multiply by the amount actually
mixed to get an extensive rate:

$$\dot{H}_{mix} = \dot{n}_{total}\,\Delta H_{mix} = 76.96 \times (-756) = -58.2\ \text{kW}$$

The negative sign means the mixture at the reference temperature sits *below* the pure
components at the reference temperature: mixing is exothermic.

**(c) Outlet temperature**

Relative to the pure liquids at 20 $^\circ$C, the inlet enthalpy rate is

$$\sum \dot{m}_{in}H_{in} = \underbrace{1.50(2.44)(20-20)}_{\text{ethanol, }=\,0}
+ \underbrace{0.80(4.18)(75-20)}_{\text{water}} = 183.9\ \text{kW}$$

The outlet stream is reached from the reference by a two-step path: mix the pure liquids
at $T_{ref}$, then heat the resulting solution from $T_{ref}$ to $T$.

$$\sum \dot{m}_{out}H_{out} = \dot{n}_{total}\Delta H_{mix} + \sum_k \dot{m}_k C_{P,k}\left(T - T_{ref}\right)$$

$$\sum_k \dot{m}_k C_{P,k} = 1.50(2.44) + 0.80(4.18) = 7.004\ \text{kW K}^{-1}$$

Setting inlet equal to outlet and solving symbolically first:

$$T = T_{ref} + \frac{\dot{m}_B C_{P,B}\left(T_B - T_{ref}\right) - \dot{n}_{total}\Delta H_{mix}}{\sum_k \dot{m}_k C_{P,k}}$$

$$T = 20 + \frac{183.9 - (-58.2)}{7.004} = 20 + \frac{242.1}{7.004} = 20 + 34.6$$

$$\boxed{T = 54.6\ ^\circ\text{C}}$$

**Check.** The mixing term entered with a *positive* sign after rearrangement, raising
$T$ — correct. The vessel is insulated, so the energy released on mixing has nowhere to
go except into the sensible heat of the stream leaving. Had the mixing been endothermic,
$\Delta H_{mix}$ would be positive and the outlet would be *cooler* than the
no-mixing case.

**(d) Comparison with Problem 5.1**

| | $T_{out}$ ($^\circ$C) |
|---|:---:|
| Neglecting $\Delta H_{mix}$ (Problem 5.1) | 46.3 |
| Including $\Delta H_{mix}$ | 54.6 |

Neglecting the enthalpy of mixing under-predicts the outlet temperature by 8.3 K, an
error of roughly 25 % on the temperature *rise* of the ethanol stream. That is not a
minor correction:

- For a **process design** — sizing a downstream cooler, or checking against a solvent
  flash point or a materials temperature limit — an 8 K error is easily enough to matter.
- Ethanol–water is a strongly non-ideal mixture. For a nearly ideal mixture (say two
  similar hydrocarbons), $\Delta H_{mix}$ is small and the assumption in Problem 5.1
  would have been perfectly defensible.

The lesson is not "never neglect mixing" but that the assumption must be *justified
against the system*, not adopted by default because it makes the arithmetic easier.

**A remaining approximation.** The sensible-heat term still used mass-weighted *pure*
component heat capacities. The heat capacity of a real ethanol–water solution is not the
weighted average of the pure values, for exactly the same reason its enthalpy is not.
Using a measured solution $C_P$ would refine the answer further.
